title: Legacy code: characterize, then refactor
summary: Code with no tests and no spec: pin what it does today with characterization tests, refactor it under their protection, then add the feature you were asked for. A Gilded-Rose-style kata.

steps.title: When there is no specification
body: Michael Feathers defines legacy code as **code without tests**. You are asked to add one small feature to a nested-`if` function that nobody understands any more. Changing it blind is how outages happen.

1. **Characterization tests** first. They do not check what the code *should* do; they record what it *does* today. Call it with an input, see the output, write that output into the assertion. Bugs included: production may depend on them.
2. Find the seams: cover each branch (use a coverage report to see the ones you missed).
3. **Refactor** in small steps, running the tests after each.
4. Only then **add the feature**, test-first, on clean code.

A quick way to write many characterization tests is a **golden master**: run the code over a grid of inputs, save the whole output once, and compare against it (Verify, ApprovalTests). Hand-written cases are clearer when the rules are few.

steps.prompt: While writing characterization tests you find that a concert ticket at quality 49 with 5 days to go ends at 50, while the product owner says it "should" be 52. What do you write in the test?
options: 50, what the code does now, with a note; raise the question separately, and change it only as a deliberate, tested change
52, because tests should describe the correct behaviour
Nothing: skip that case until the product owner decides
Assert that the value is between 50 and 52
steps.explain: Characterization tests protect today's behaviour during a refactor. Fixing behaviour in the same step mixes two changes, so when something breaks you cannot tell which caused it. (Here the code is right anyway: quality never goes above 50.)

steps.title: Pin the legacy pantry with characterization tests
prompt: The pantry shop's nightly job ages its stock. Nobody dares touch it. It is compiled beside your tests:
public class Item { public string Name = ""; public int SellIn; public int Quality; }

Before anyone refactors it, write `public class PantryCharacterizationTests`: at least **10** cases (a `[Theory]` with a helper is the fast way) that record what one day does to each kind of item: name, `SellIn` and `Quality` before, and both after. Find the edges yourself by reading the branches.
Six planted bugs, each a typical slip someone makes while refactoring this code.
starter: static Item OneDay(string name, int sellIn, int quality)
var item = new Item { Name = name, SellIn = sellIn, Quality = quality };
public void One_day_later(string name, int sellIn, int quality, int sellInAfter, int qualityAfter)
solution: static Item OneDay(string name, int sellIn, int quality)
var item = new Item { Name = name, SellIn = sellIn, Quality = quality };
public void One_day_later(string name, int sellIn, int quality, int sellInAfter, int qualityAfter)

target: public class Item { public string Name = ""; public int SellIn; public int Quality; }

mutants.name: tickets gain only 2 a day in the last five days
tickets keep their value after the concert
a ticket can go above 50
mutants.hint: Try a ticket at quality 49 with 10 days to go.

mutants.name: ordinary items lose only 1 a day after their date
sea salt gets older
mutants.hint: Check the SellIn of Sea Salt after a day, not only its quality.

hints: Read the branches as a list of item kinds: ordinary items, Aged Cheddar, Sea Salt, Concert Ticket. Each kind needs a case before and after its sell-by date.
Concert tickets have three speeds: more than 10 days (+1), 10 to 6 days (+2), 5 days or fewer (+3), and they drop to 0 after the concert. Test 10 and 5 days exactly.
Do not forget the limits: an ordinary item at quality 0, a cheddar at 50, a ticket at 49 with 10 days left. And assert Sea Salt's SellIn too.
steps.explain: Twelve rows now describe the function better than its code does. They are the safety net for the next step: a refactor that keeps all twelve green has not changed what the shop sees.

steps.title: Refactor under the net
body: With the characterization tests green, restructure in small steps. One shape that reads like the rules:

Careful: after `SellIn--`, the old "less than 11" becomes "less than 10". Exactly that kind of shift is what the characterization tests are there to catch. And `Math.Max(50, item.Quality)` keeps an item that is somehow above 50 where it was, as the old code did; a test case documents it.

steps.prompt: Refactoring step or behaviour change? Only refactoring steps belong in the refactor commit.
buckets: Behaviour change (needs its own test first)
items: Replace the nested ifs with a switch on the item name
Decrement SellIn at the top instead of the middle
Let Fresh Herbs lose 2 a day
Extract a method per item kind
Cap Aged Cheddar at 60 instead of 50
steps.explain: A refactor changes structure, never behaviour, so the characterization tests must stay green the whole way. New rules come after, each with a failing test first.

steps.title: Refactor, then add fresh herbs
prompt: Now refactor `Pantry.UpdateQuality` into code you would be happy to review, and add the feature the shop asked for:
> **Fresh Herbs** lose quality **twice as fast** as ordinary items (2 a day, 4 a day after their date), never below 0.

Write the whole `Item` class and `Pantry` class (keep `Item` exactly as it is), plus your own `public class FreshHerbsTests` with at least **3** tests for the new rule, written first. **Run checks** also runs the team's characterization tests (`PantryCharacterization`), so any behaviour change for the old items shows up as a red row.
starter: public class Item { public string Name = ""; public int SellIn; public int Quality; }
solution: public class Item { public string Name = ""; public int SellIn; public int Quality; }
static Item OneDay(int sellIn, int quality)
var item = new Item { Name = "Fresh Herbs", SellIn = sellIn, Quality = quality };
template: static (int SellIn, int Quality) OneDay(string name, int sellIn, int quality)
var item = new Item { Name = name, SellIn = sellIn, Quality = quality };
public void One_day_later(string name, int sellIn, int quality, int sellInAfter, int qualityAfter)
hints: Move one rule at a time and press Run checks after each move: the characterization rows tell you at once if behaviour changed.
After decrementing `SellIn` first, the ticket thresholds become `SellIn < 10` (was 11) and `SellIn < 5` (was 6).
Fresh herbs are one more arm in the switch: `"Fresh Herbs" => expired ? -4 : -2,`, and `Math.Clamp` keeps it at 0 or above.
steps.explain: The feature took one line because the refactor came first. That is the order seniors insist on: make the change easy (with the tests protecting you), then make the easy change.
